Create a 16-bit color pixel image of the eiffel tower as a jpg

Deliver the result as image and/or video files, working in the current directory.
- Save the finished files in ./output/. Only what is in ./output/ is published as the result.
- Formats: images as .png, .jpg, .webp, .gif or .svg; videos as .mp4 or .webm. At most 8 files,
  each under 2 MB; videos at most 10 seconds.
- Tools available on this machine: python3 3.9.6 (standard library only), node 26.11.1 (no npm packages), ffmpeg 9.0.2, ffprobe 9.0.2. Don't install packages or download anything.
- Keep any code you write to make the files (it's published as the source), but delete
  intermediate files such as rendered frames when you're done.
- Only create or edit files inside the current directory.
- Finish with a short summary of what you made.

I'll paint the tower on a small pixel grid using RGB565 colors, then convert it to JPG with ffmpeg. JPG stores 8 bits per channel, so the 16-bit look comes from the RGB565 palette rather than a 16-bit file format.

The file generated at 640×800 and is 66 KB. Next I'll view it to check the tower's shape.

The image is ready: `output/eiffel_tower_16bit.jpg`, 640×800, 66 KB.

It's a pixel-art Eiffel Tower silhouetted against a sunset with the sun behind it, clouds, a treeline, a lawn and the Seine. I drew it on a 160×200 grid and scaled each pixel up 4×.

"16-bit color" is the one part I had to interpret. Every pixel is snapped to RGB565 (65,536 colors, 5-6-5 bits per channel), and the sky gradient is ordered-dithered the way 16-bit hardware did. JPEG stores 8 bits per channel, so the file itself can't be a true 16-bit image; the 16-bit character comes from the palette.

The generator script is `output/make_eiffel_16bit.py`. It uses only the standard library, and it pipes the image straight to ffmpeg, so no intermediate files were created. Run it with `python3 output/make_eiffel_16bit.py <out.jpg>` to regenerate.
